questions.stem: Which helicopter control changes the pitch of all main-rotor blades at the same time to make the aircraft climb or descend?
options: The collective
The cyclic
The anti-torque pedals
The throttle
questions.explanation: The collective raises or lowers the pitch of every main-rotor blade together, changing total lift so the helicopter climbs or descends. The cyclic tilts the rotor disc; the pedals control yaw.

questions.stem: The correct recovery from vortex ring state is to:
options: Gain airspeed and lower collective
Raise collective to add more power
Enter a steeper vertical descent
Hold the hover and wait it out
questions.explanation: Recovery means flying out of the descending air by gaining forward airspeed and reducing collective; adding power only feeds the vortex and worsens the descent.

questions.stem: Ground resonance begins on touchdown while rotor RPM is still in the normal operating range. The recommended action is to:
options: Hold the aircraft down with forward cyclic
Lift off to a hover to break ground contact
Close the throttle and apply the rotor brake
Lower the collective fully and hold position
questions.explanation: With RPM in the normal range, lifting off to a hover removes the ground contact that feeds the oscillation, letting the blades realign. Closing the throttle and lowering the collective is the choice only when RPM is too low to fly.

questions.stem: Before a VFR helicopter enters Class C airspace, the pilot must:
options: Receive the words "cleared into" from ATC
File a VFR flight plan with flight service
Establish two-way radio contact with ATC
Hold an instrument rating and clearance
questions.explanation: Class C requires two-way radio communication before entry, which is established when ATC answers using the aircraft's call sign. An explicit "cleared into" clearance is the Class B requirement.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Swans are the heaviest birds capable of powered flight.
Migrating birds navigate across oceans using the stars.
Bird flight relies on physical principles like lift and drag.
Feathers keep birds warm as well as helping them fly.
questions.passage:
Watch a gull hang almost motionless above a harbor and it is easy to assume that flight is effortless. In truth, every soaring bird is solving a constant physical problem: how to stay aloft without falling and how to move forward without stalling. The secret lies mostly in the shape of the wing. A bird's wing is curved on top and flatter underneath, a form called an airfoil. As the wing slices through the air, the flow moving over the curved upper surface travels faster than the flow beneath it. This difference in speed lowers the pressure above the wing, and the higher pressure below pushes the wing upward. That upward push is what pilots and biologists alike call lift.

Lift alone is not enough. A bird must also overcome drag, the resistance created as its body pushes air aside. Larger, heavier birds such as swans need powerful chest muscles and rapid wingbeats to generate the thrust that carries them forward. Smaller birds spend less energy per beat but must flap far more often. Soaring species, by contrast, have learned to let the atmosphere do much of the work. They ride columns of warm rising air, called thermals, spiraling upward without a single flap, then glide slowly downward to the next thermal.

Feathers make these feats possible. The long, stiff feathers at the wingtip can be spread like fingers to reduce the swirling turbulence that would otherwise drag a bird backward. When a bird needs to slow down to land, it tilts its wings sharply, trading smooth airflow for a burst of braking resistance. Understanding these principles did not merely satisfy curiosity; it gave early aircraft designers a working model. Nature, it turned out, had been refining the airfoil for millions of years before any engineer sketched a wing.
questions.explanation: The passage explains lift, drag, and how these principles gave aircraft designers a working model. The other options state real-world facts the text never makes.

questions.stem: The passage implies that helicopters are especially valuable for rescue work because they can
options: hover and operate without needing a runway.
fly much faster than any fixed-wing plane.
carry far heavier loads than any airplane.
stay airborne far longer without refueling.
questions.passage:
The dream of rising straight up into the air is older than the airplane. Sketches of screw-like flying machines appear in notebooks from the Renaissance, and children in Europe and Asia had long played with spinning toy rotors carved from wood. Turning that dream into a machine that could carry a person, however, took centuries, and it defeated many capable inventors. The problem was not simply getting a rotor to lift a craft off the ground. The deeper difficulty was control.

A fixed-wing airplane, once moving forward, is reasonably stable. A helicopter hovering in place is not. As the main rotor spins one way, it tries to spin the fuselage the opposite way, threatening to send the whole craft into a hopeless twirl. Early experimenters tried mounting two rotors turning in opposite directions to cancel this effect. The breakthrough that made the modern helicopter practical came when designers added a small vertical rotor on the tail. By pushing sideways, the tail rotor counteracts the twisting force and, when adjusted, lets the pilot swing the nose left or right at will.

Just as important was a mechanism allowing the pitch of each blade to change as it rotates, so that lift could be tilted in any direction. With it, a pilot could move forward, backward, or sideways, or hold a steady hover. Once these controls were mastered, the helicopter found work that no airplane could match. It could lift a stranded climber from a cliff, drop supplies where no runway existed, or lower a rescuer onto a sinking ship. What had begun as a whimsical toy and a Renaissance daydream became, within a single lifetime, one of the most versatile machines ever built, valued less for its speed than for its stubborn refusal to need a runway at all.
questions.explanation: The passage lists rescue tasks and ends by valuing the helicopter for its refusal to need a runway, which depends on its ability to hover.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Pilots must trust instruments because the inner ear can misread long turns.
Experienced pilots no longer feel the false sensations that trouble students.
The semicircular canals sense rotation accurately in all flight conditions.
Pilots should avoid any turn that lasts longer than about twenty seconds.
questions.passage:
The inner ear contains three fluid-filled semicircular canals, set roughly at right angles to one another, that let the brain sense rotation. When the head turns, the fluid lags behind the canal walls and bends tiny hair cells, signaling motion. The system works well for the brief turns of everyday life. In flight it can be dangerously misleading.

The problem is that the canals detect changes in rotation, not rotation itself. If a pilot enters a gradual turn and holds it, the fluid soon catches up with the canal walls and the hair cells straighten. Within perhaps twenty seconds the brain concludes that the turn has stopped, although the aircraft is still banked. If the pilot then rolls level, the fluid moves again, and the brain reports a turn in the opposite direction. A pilot without a visible horizon may lean, or even roll back into the original bank, to make the false sensation go away.

Training cannot switch these sensations off. Experienced pilots feel them as strongly as students do. What training provides is a habit: when the body and the instruments disagree, believe the instruments. That habit is easy to state and surprisingly hard to keep, because the false sensation feels completely real at the moment it matters most.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how the canals misread sustained turns and concludes that pilots must rely on instruments. It says experienced pilots still feel the illusions and never advises avoiding long turns.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, an aircraft flying through a cloud of large supercooled droplets would most likely collect ice that is
options: rough and milky, with trapped air.
thin and harmless, as large drops bounce off.
limited to the windscreen, not the wings.
clear, and spread back over the surface.
questions.passage:
Water does not always freeze at 0°C. In clouds, tiny droplets can remain liquid at temperatures well below freezing, sometimes colder than -20°C, because they lack a particle of dust or ice around which a crystal can begin to grow. Such droplets are called supercooled, and they stay liquid only as long as nothing disturbs them.

An aircraft is a very large disturbance. When it flies through a cloud of supercooled droplets, the droplets strike the leading edges of the wings, the windscreen and, on a helicopter, the rotor blades, and they freeze almost at once. Small droplets tend to freeze the instant they hit, trapping air and forming rough, milky rime ice. Larger droplets freeze more slowly; they spread back across the surface before hardening into clear ice, which is heavier, harder to see and harder to remove.

Ice harms flight less through its weight than through its shape. Even a thin, rough layer on a wing or rotor blade disrupts the smooth flow of air over the airfoil, cutting lift and adding drag. For a helicopter the problem is especially serious, because its rotor blades are its wings, and ice on them raises the power needed simply to stay in the air. Many helicopters are not certified to fly into known icing conditions at all.
questions.explanation: Larger droplets freeze more slowly and spread back across the surface before hardening into clear ice. Rough, milky rime comes from small droplets.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 14 cm long and 9 cm wide. What is its perimeter?
A driver goes to a town at 30 mph and returns along the same route at 60 mph. What is the average speed for the round trip?
options: 45 mph
90 mph
40 mph
50 mph
questions.explanation: Round-trip average speed = 2(30)(60)/(30+60) = 3600/90 = 40 mph (not the simple average).

questions.stem: A mechanic pushes a tool cart with a constant horizontal force of 60 N over a distance of 5 m. How much work does the mechanic do on the cart?
questions.explanation: Work = force x distance = 60 N x 5 m = 300 J. Dividing (12) or adding (65) the values, or inserting a stray 1/2 factor (150), all give wrong results.

questions.stem: A 10 kg toolbox is lifted onto a shelf 3 m above the floor. Using g = 9.8 m/s^2, how much gravitational potential energy does it gain?
questions.topic: Gravitational potential energy (PE = m g h)
questions.explanation: PE = m g h = 10 x 9.8 x 3 = 294 J. Leaving out g gives 30 (m x h); inserting a stray 1/2 gives 147; leaving out h gives 98 (m x g).

questions.stem: In a block-and-tackle system, 5 rope sections directly support the load. Ignoring friction, what effort is needed to lift a 1,000 N load at constant speed?
questions.explanation: For an ideal pulley system the mechanical advantage equals the number of supporting rope sections (5). Effort = load / MA = 1,000 / 5 = 200 N. Multiplying by 5 gives 5,000; ignoring the system gives 1,000.

questions.stem: A motor supplies 8 N.m of torque to a 12-tooth driver gear that meshes with a 48-tooth driven gear. Ignoring losses, what is the output torque at the driven gear, and how does its speed compare to the driver?
options: 32 N.m, and it turns slower
2 N.m, and it turns faster
32 N.m, and it turns faster
8 N.m, at the same speed
questions.explanation: Gear ratio = driven/driver teeth = 48/12 = 4. A larger driven gear multiplies torque by the ratio (8 x 4 = 32 N.m) and reduces speed by the same ratio, so it turns slower. Torque and speed trade off inversely; power is conserved.
